title: Loving for others
hook: a friend's good news, a half-second pause, and a hadith that walks straight into it

segments.voice: Yesterday, silat al-rahim, and your line: keep the ties. Did a message go out to someone you'd let drift? Today, a sentence about what you want, and who else you want it for. Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.

A friend gets the job you both applied for. Or the apartment. Or the news you've been waiting years to hear yourself. The text arrives, and for some people there's a half-second before typing congratulations where something tightens. Nobody chooses that half-second. But there's a short hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari that walks right into it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. Today: the half-second, and what this hadith asks of it.
screen: `THE FRIEND GETS THE JOB.` → `A HALF-SECOND PAUSE.` → `LOVE FOR HIM WHAT YOU LOVE.`

segments.voice: First, look at how the sentence is built. It doesn't say: stop wanting good things. It starts from what a person already wants for himself. Health. Ease. Being forgiven. A good name. Rest. That's the measuring stick. Whatever you'd be glad to receive, want it for someone else too. The hadith uses your own wanting as the ruler. Second, the verb. The hadith doesn't say give, or share, though those may follow. It says love: yuhibbu, he loves. It's about what the heart wants. You can't always hand someone what they need. You can always want it for them. Third, who counts. The hadith in Bukhari says his brother. A narration in Sahih Muslim gives the same words with his brother, or, the narrator adds, his neighbor. And a narration in al-Nasa'i spells out what kind of thing is meant: of good. So this isn't loving for others whatever you happen to crave. It's the good: guidance, health, mercy, the thing that would actually help. Fourth, the strong opening: none of you believes. Some commentators read this as faith not yet complete, not as a person leaving Islam. The hadith points at a gap between believing in words and believing all the way down, and it locates that gap in a very ordinary place: what happens inside when someone else gets the good thing. The half-second is where the hadith does its work.
screen: `YOUR OWN WANTING IS THE RULER.` · `YUHIBBU: LOVE, NOT ONLY GIVE.` · `BROTHER, NEIGHBOR: OF GOOD.` · `FAITH, ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: The practice: want for someone what you want. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing you've been hoping for lately. Not a list. One thing: rest, a good result, a door opening. Hold it a moment. Now bring someone to mind. A friend, a coworker, maybe the one whose good news stung a little. Picture them receiving that same thing. See their face when it arrives. Stay with it until the wanting feels real, or at least a little closer. If you pray, you can ask for it for them, by name, before you ask for yourself. The bell holds the time.
Loving for others. From the hadith in Bukhari: wanting for another person the good you want for yourself, as part of faith itself. Today's word.

Your line: love it for them. Today, when someone else's good news arrives, say to them the words you'd hope to hear if it were yours. Tomorrow, contentment with little. Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Muslims cite this hadith as a measure of faith: wanting for others the good one wants for oneself, and making du'a for others' good.

myth: the hadith asks you to stop wanting good things for yourself
it starts from what you want for yourself and uses that as the measure for others.
the hadith's verb is love, not only give
yuhibbu, he loves: the heart's wanting comes first.
some commentators read 'none of you believes' as faith not yet complete
they read it as incomplete faith, not as leaving Islam.

fork.setup: your friend gets the very thing you were hoping for. the hadith in Bukhari gives you a measure for the next moment. what is it?
options: say nothing until the feeling passes.
want for them what you'd want for yourself.
point out it could just as easily have been you.
fork.reveal: none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself: your own wanting becomes the measure for theirs.

original.note: Arabic: he loves. the verb at the heart of the hadith (Bukhari 13).

trapdoor: what you thought: be happy for people.
what it means: want for another person, really want, the good you want for yourself, because that is part of faith.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 13 with Muslim 45's 'or his neighbor' and al-Nasa'i's 'of good': the circle is wide, and the thing loved is good.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 13 (none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself)
Sahih Muslim 45 (for his brother, or for his neighbor)
Sunan al-Nasa'i 5017 (what he loves for himself of good)

notes: Hadith numbers to confirm: Bukhari 13; Muslim 45 (the 'or his neighbor' wording, with the narrator's doubt); al-Nasa'i 5017 ('min al-khayr').
Teach says commentators explain 'none of you believes' as incomplete faith. Keeper to confirm this phrasing.
Hook says 'for some people there's a half-second' of tightness; kept to 'some people' so the listener isn't told what they feel.
Index word is the title head 'Loving for others'; kept exactly.
